newsitem.title: GERMANY: Aircraft in hunt for kidnapped German businessman.
newsitem.headline: Aircraft in hunt for kidnapped German businessman.

text.p: Two German military fighters equipped with heat-seeking devices on Friday scoured a densly-wooded area as part of an intensive hunt for a kidnapped Frankfurt multi-millionaire.

Police said the planes were covering the Taunus region about 50 km (30 miles) west of Frankfurt, where about 500 police equipped with machetes and sniffer dogs were searching the countryside for missing businessman Jakub Fiszman.
Investigators were tipped off about the area by one of two suspects remanded in custody on suspicion of helping to kidnap Fiszman, who has been missing since October 1.
Police said they were becoming more pessimistic about finding Fiszman, whose family's fortune has been estimated by police to be more than 400 million marks ($260 million).
The 40-year-old businessman is best known for financing the failed Frankfurt production of the rock musical "Tommy".
"We have no concrete evidence that he is dead but we are more pessimistic than we were yesterday," police spokesman Ulrich Petri said at the scene of the search.
Since his abduction, the only word from 40-year-old Fiszman, who needs medicine for chronic food allergies, has been a telephone call to a friend he made on October 2.
Police said the two suspects in custody are a 48-year-old man, Rainer Koerppen and his 26-year-old son, Sven. Three other people detained as part of the probe were released on Friday.
Prosecutor Rainer Schilling said Sven Koerppen had confessed to investigators that he and his father took Fiszman on October 4 to the area now being searched by police.
Before entering the wooded area, Rainer Koerppen made his son get out of the car and then drove off with Fiszman.
"The son said his father apparently wanted to take Fiszman to an area where he would not be able to escape," Schilling said.
Police were still searching for one or more suspects in the kidnapping, which has attracted media attention as the second abduction this year of a wealthy German businessman.
Police lifted a news blackout on the kidnapping last weekend in the hope that the public could helping to find Fiszman
Fiszman's brother Georg paid a ransom of four million marks on October 10, but his kidnappers reneged on an agreement and failed to free him the following day.
Police recovered most of the ransom on Wednesday in the garden of a flat in Wiesbaden owned by Koerppen's parents.
